name: Fangzheng YAN

papers.title: PRTS: A Primitive Reasoning and Tasking System via Contrastive Representations
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic control via strong visual-linguistic priors. However, existing VLAs predominantly frame pretraining as supervised behavior cloning, overlooking the fundamental nature of robot learning as a goal-reaching process that requires understanding temporal task progress. We present \textbf{PRTS} (\textbf{P}rimitive \textbf{R}easoning and \textbf{T}asking \textbf{S}ystem), a VLA foundation model that reformulates pretraining through Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning. By treating language instructions as goals and employing contrastive reinforcement learning, PRTS learns a unified embedding space where the inner product of state-action and goal embeddings approximates the log-discounted goal occupancy, the probability of reaching the language-specified goal from the current state-action, quantitatively assessing physical feasibility beyond static semantic matching. PRTS draws this dense goal-reachability supervision directly from offline trajectories without reward annotations, and folds it into the VLM backbone via a role-aware causal mask, incurring negligible overhead over vanilla behavior cloning. This paradigm endows the high-level reasoning system with intrinsic goal reachability awareness, bridging semantic reasoning and temporal task progress, and further benefits goal-conditioned action prediction. Pretrained on 167B tokens of diverse manipulation and embodied-reasoning data, PRTS reaches state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and a real-world suite of 14 complex tasks, with particularly substantial gains on long-horizon, contact-rich, and zero-shot novel-instruction settings, confirming that injecting goal-reachability awareness significantly improves both execution success and long-horizon planning of general-purpose robotic foundation policies.

papers.title: Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning with Human Interventions for Precise Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels.

papers.title: VISTA: Vision-Grounded and Physics-Validated Adaptation of UMI data for VLA Training
papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable data collection without target-robot teleoperation, but UMI-style demonstrations are not directly suited for large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) training. We identify the challenge of training VLA models from UMI-collected data as a dual adaptation problem: (i) wrist-mounted fisheye observations are misaligned with the visual distributions of pretrained vision-language models, and (ii) human-collected trajectories are not guaranteed to be executable under target-robot embodiment constraints. To mitigate this challenge, we present VISTA, a framework that adapts UMI-collected data to VLA training through fisheye-aligned visual grounding and embodiment-conditioned trajectory validation. UMI-VQA supplies vision-language supervision under wrist-mounted fisheye observations, while trajectory validation scores human-collected demonstrations by continuity, self-collision risk, and execution fidelity to select physically plausible action supervision before training. VISTA then uses the adapted visual-language data and validated trajectories in a two-stage VLA training procedure. Experiments show that UMI-VQA improves policy performance over action-only training and standard-view VQA, while validation scores are predictive of real-robot deployment success. Across UMI-style simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, VISTA consistently improves over strong VLA baselines including $\pi_{0.5}$, LingBot-VLA, and Wall-X. We will release the pipeline, datasets, and pretrained model.
